description: Mater Amabilis Year 5 living books curriculum for grade 5. The Plutarch rotation continues, American history moves from the colonies toward the founding era, and written narration becomes the primary mode across most subjects.

books.title: Adam of the Road
books.author: Elizabeth Janet Gray
books.subject: living_books
books.notes: A minstrel boy's travels across medieval England searching for his lost dog and father. Newbery Medal winner. 'What does Adam learn about home along the way?'

books.title: The Door in the Wall
books.author: Marguerite de Angeli
books.subject: living_books
books.notes: A boy who cannot walk finds a different kind of usefulness and courage. 'What was the door in the wall, really?'

books.title: The Voyage of the Dawn Treader
books.author: C. S. Lewis
books.subject: living_books
books.notes: Each island tests a different temptation — greed, vanity, despair. Pairs well with this year's growing emphasis on written narration of character change. 'What changed Eustace from the inside, not just the outside?'

books.title: Plutarch's Lives (selected passages, continuing rotation)
books.author: Plutarch
books.subject: history
books.notes: Continuing the multi-year rotation begun in Year 3. Read slowly, one incident at a time. 'Was this choice virtuous, or only effective?'

books.title: The Story of the Thirteen Colonies
books.author: H. A. Guerber
books.subject: history
books.notes: Guerber's narrative history moves from early settlement toward the founding era, picking up where Year 4's George Washington's World left off. 'What made each colony's founding different from the others?'

books.title: Trial and Triumph: Stories from Church History (continuing)
books.author: Richard Hannula
books.subject: saints
books.notes: Continuing the rotation. 'What did this person risk, and why did they think it was worth it?'

books.title: Madam How and Lady Why (second half)
books.author: Charles Kingsley
books.subject: science
books.notes: Continuing from Year 4's first half. Read a chapter, then look for a real example outdoors if possible. 'What question would you ask Madam How this time?'

books.title: Archimedes and the Door of Science
books.author: Jeanne Bendick
books.subject: science
books.notes: A short, lively biography of Archimedes and the birth of scientific reasoning in the ancient world. Ties naturally to this term's Plutarch reading on ancient Greece and Rome.

books.title: Handbook of Nature Study (continuing reference)
books.author: Anna Botsford Comstock
books.subject: nature_study
books.notes: A reference, not a read-aloud — consult for whatever the child has just found outside. Pair every entry with a nature journal sketch.

subject_plans.art_music: Composer: Franz Schubert — lyrical, singable melodies (try 'The Trout' quintet), a warm middle ground between Classical clarity and Romantic feeling. Artist: Albrecht Dürer — precise, richly detailed engravings and woodcuts that reward slow, close looking. Ask what the child notices only on a second look. Poet: Alfred, Lord Tennyson — narrative and historical poems with strong rhythm (The Charge of the Light Brigade), pairing naturally with this year's history reading.
subject_plans.greek: Year 5 scope (grade 5) — words to phrases. The student reads short Greek phrases rather than single words and can say what each word is doing: "ego eimi he hodos"; "te elpidi chairontes". The definite article is introduced — Greek uses ho, he, to constantly where English drops it, and noticing that unlocks whole verses. The Great Commandment is now held as one sentence rather than two halves, and the student can find agapeseis in it and connect it to agape. Everything in this year is the shared inheritance of all Christian traditions — the Greek New Testament, the theological virtues, and the ordinary vocabulary of the faith — so a Protestant, Catholic, or Orthodox family can teach it in full. Introduce nothing specific to one tradition here (devotion to the saints or to Mary, the sacraments, prayers for the dead, icons, a particular church's authority or structure), and take no position on which Greek manuscript tradition is correct: every text supplied reads the same in both. Send any doctrinal question that divides Christian traditions to the family's own pastor, priest, or minister. All Greek quoted must come from the verbatim block supplied in the session — never recited from memory, never composed — and always shown with its transliteration and English.
subject_plans.language_arts: Grade 5: written narration is now the primary mode for most subjects, not the exception. Dictation passages grow longer and more complex. Grammar covers more sophisticated sentence structures (compound and complex sentences), and the student begins a simple outline before narrating a longer passage.
subject_plans.latin: Year 5 scope (grade 5) — from words to phrases. The student meets short complete Latin phrases rather than single words, and can say what each word in them is doing: 'Ego sum via, et veritas, et vita'; 'Spe gaudentes'; 'Deo gratias'. Nominative and accusative are named for the first time, taught from the Great Commandment itself, which the student now holds as one sentence rather than two halves. Copywork gives way to the student writing a known phrase from memory and checking it against the printed text — their own proofreading, not a graded test. Everything in this year is the shared inheritance of all Christian traditions — the Vulgate, the theological virtues, and the ordinary vocabulary of the faith — so a family of any Christian tradition can teach it in full. Introduce nothing specific to one tradition here (devotion to the saints or to Mary, the sacraments, prayers for the dead, a particular church's authority or structure); a family that wants that has Saints & Catechism as its own subject. Send any doctrinal question that divides Christian traditions to the family's own pastor, priest, or minister. All Latin quoted must come from the verbatim block supplied in the session — never recited from memory, never composed.
subject_plans.logic: Year 5 scope (grade 5) — contradiction and testability. The child can now notice when two things they've said cannot both be true, and hold that as interesting rather than embarrassing. Add the question that quietly does the most work in the whole subject: "what would change your mind?" — which teaches that a belief worth holding is one that could in principle be checked, and gently exposes a claim built so it can never be wrong. Logic serves truth and charity, never winning an argument: teach the student to test their own reasoning first and to state the strongest version of the other side fairly before criticizing it. Never coach a child in arguing against their own parents' instructions or authority — a disagreement at home belongs to the family, not to a logic lesson. Do not rule on political, moral, or religious questions however logically they are framed; teach the form with neutral examples and send the substance to the student's own parents and their own pastor, priest, or minister. Declining to rule is not the same as calling the matter unsettled: say that it belongs to their family and their church, which teach something definite about it, rather than that thoughtful people disagree. On a political question reasonable people genuinely do differ and you may say so; on a moral or religious one do not characterize the landscape at all, because presenting a settled conviction of theirs as a live dispute takes a side while appearing not to. Work only from the arguments supplied in the session — never invent a syllogism or a fallacy example, since an invalid argument can look perfectly sound and the student cannot yet catch that.
subject_plans.mathematics: Grade 5 scope: decimal place value and all four operations with decimals; multiplying AND dividing fractions; adding and subtracting with unlike denominators; the order of operations applied to longer expressions; volume of rectangular prisms; converting between measurement units; plotting points on a coordinate plane; area of polygons. This is the last year of pure arithmetic — everything here is assumed finished when pre-algebra starts. Mater Amabilis approach: real-world problems (recipes, measurements, maps) before the abstract notation.
subject_plans.morning_time: Scripture with more substantive discussion of its meaning, a hymn or folk song, and Tennyson for poetry. Connect briefly to this term's history rotation — the colonies, or Adam of the Road's medieval England.
subject_plans.scripture: Year 5 scope — the prophets and the Psalms: Isaiah's call and the servant passages; Jeremiah's laments; Ezekiel's visions; the twelve minor prophets in brief; the Psalms as Israel's prayer book — lament, thanksgiving, praise, trust. Gospels: the miracles as signs, and the 'I am' sayings in John. Charlotte Mason approach: read a psalm aloud and ask which kind of prayer it is and why. Poetry rewards being heard before being analysed. Canon and translation are the family's own: follow whatever Bible they are reading and never assert that one tradition's canon, chapter ordering, or translation is the correct one. Teach the narrative and the moral law the text plainly states; leave denomination-specific doctrine — sacramental theology, church governance, a particular catechism's structure — to the family's own pastor, priest, or minister.
